summary: Redefines selected ICMP messages so they can carry more than the original information. An extension structure at the end of the message, with its own header and objects, holds extra data that applications may require. It is a standards-track document.

plainLanguage.summary: The old error notes had little room to write on. This adds extra pages at the back, so a note can carry more helpful details.

questions: what is the icmp extension structure
why does icmp need a length attribute
how does traceroute use icmp extensions
subtitle: How ICMP error messages got a length field and an extension structure so they can carry extra information.

tldr.problem: Some ICMP error messages end with a variable-length copy of the original datagram that has no length field, so nothing could be appended to them without making them unparsable.
tldr.mechanism: Eight previously reserved bits become a length attribute for the original datagram field, and an extension structure (a header plus objects) is appended after it.
tldr.outcome: ICMP error messages can carry extra information, such as for traceroute, while older implementations keep working. RFC 8335 later updated this RFC.

today: RFC 4884 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 792 and RFC 4443, and it has itself been updated by RFC 8335; it has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: The Problem with the Original Datagram Field
sections.content:
RFC 4884 redefines selected ICMPv4 and ICMPv6 messages to include an extension structure and a length attribute. The extension structure lets protocol designers make an ICMP message carry additional information.

The underlying problem is that every message addressed here includes an original datagram field holding the initial octets of the datagram that caused the error. The field has variable length, but the message has no field giving that length. Software infers it from the total ICMP message length, so appending an extension structure would leave software unable to tell where the original datagram ends and the extension begins.

The document defines only the extension header and a common object header. It defines no extension objects itself. It notes that other memos append information to the ICMP Time Exceeded message for use by traceroute, and that appending is preferable to emitting two messages whenever a packet is dropped because of TTL expiry.
sections.plainLanguage: Imagine a note that ends with a copy of your letter but never says how long that copy is. If you staple on extra pages, nobody can tell where the copy stops.

sections.title: Summary of Changes
sections.content:
An extension structure MAY be appended to ICMPv4 Destination Unreachable, Time Exceeded and Parameter Problem messages, and to ICMPv6 Destination Unreachable and Time Exceeded messages. It MUST NOT be appended to other ICMP messages. ICMPv6 Packet Too Big and Parameter Problem are excluded because they lack space for a length attribute.

When an extension structure is appended, the original datagram field MUST contain at least 128 octets, zero padded if the original was shorter. In ICMPv4 it MUST also be zero padded to a 32-bit boundary, and in ICMPv6 to a 64-bit boundary. Future ICMP messages SHOULD say whether they support the mechanism, and it is recommended that all new messages do.
sections.plainLanguage: Only some kinds of error notes get the new back pages. The copy of the original letter must be at least 128 octets long, padded with zeros if needed.

sections.title: The Length Attribute
sections.content:
The new length attribute is 8 bits and records the length of the padded original datagram field. It is taken from reserved octets that were previously required to be zero. In ICMPv4 it sits in the sixth octet of the message and counts 32-bit words. In ICMPv6 it sits in the fifth octet and counts 64-bit words.

It applies to ICMPv4 Destination Unreachable (type 3), Time Exceeded (type 11) and Parameter Problem (type 12), and to ICMPv6 Destination Unreachable (type 1) and Time Exceeded (type 3). The length attribute MUST be specified when the extension structure is appended. All other fields keep the syntax and semantics of RFC 792 or RFC 4443. In the ICMPv4 Destination Unreachable message, the Next-Hop MTU bits are shown only to demonstrate they are not available for assignment.
sections.plainLanguage: A small number is written in a spare box in the note's header. It says how long the copy of the original letter is, so the reader knows where the extra pages start.

sections.title: Backwards Compatibility
sections.content:
Some ICMP implementations produced between 1999 and publication already send a non-compliant form of these extensions: exactly 128 octets of original datagram, correct checksums, but no length attribute. Applications fall into three groups: classic (do not parse extensions), non-compliant (parse extensions but assume exactly 128 octets) and compliant (follow this document). The RFC walks through each pairing.

The 128-octet minimum exists so that extensions begin at least 128 octets into the field. Classic applications are then affected only if they process the 129th octet of the original datagram, and the RFC identifies only two such applications, with minimal effect. A non-compliant application parses compliant extensions correctly only if the original datagram field is exactly 128 octets. The whole message must stay within the minimum reassembly buffer size, 576 octets for ICMPv4 or 1280 octets for ICMPv6.

A compliant application that sees a length attribute of zero MUST conclude there are no extensions. To ease transition, compliant traceroute implementations MUST include a non-default mode that also interprets non-compliant responses by looking for a valid extension header at a fixed location after 128 octets. The RFC also argues extensions do not interfere with NAT, since a NAT should modify only the leading octets of the original datagram.
sections.plainLanguage: Some old programs already staple pages on after exactly 128 octets without saying so. New programs read the length number, and a special mode lets them also understand the old way.

sections.title: The Extension Structure and Objects
sections.content:
The extension structure contains exactly one extension header followed by one or more objects. Software MAY process selected objects and ignore others, and an unrecognized object does not make the message malformed. The total ICMP message, extensions included, MUST NOT exceed the minimum reassembly buffer size.

The 4-byte extension header has a 4-bit Version (version 2), 12 reserved bits that must be 0, and a 16-bit Checksum, the one's complement of the one's complement sum of the structure with the checksum field set to zero. An all-zero checksum means none was transmitted.

Each object is made of 32-bit words: a header with a 16-bit Length (in octets, header and payload included), an 8-bit Class-Num naming the object class and an 8-bit C-Type naming the sub-type, followed by the payload.
sections.plainLanguage: The extra pages start with a cover sheet saying which version of the rules is used and a check number. Each page after it says how long it is and what kind of page it is.

sections.title: Security and IANA Considerations
sections.content:
Software receiving an ICMP message must check it for syntactic correctness, and the extension checksum must be verified. Improperly specified length attributes and other syntax problems may result in buffer overruns. The memo does not define when a router sends an ICMP message, so it adds no new denial-of-service exposure, though routers may need to limit the rate at which they send ICMP messages.

IANA has established a registry of ICMP extension object classes and class sub-types. No values are assigned in this document. Object classes 0xF7 to 0xFF are reserved for private use, and class values are assigned first-come-first-served. The document defining a new class defines the policy for its sub-types.
sections.plainLanguage: Always check that the length numbers make sense before reading on, or a bad note could confuse your program. A public list keeps track of the kinds of extra pages.

fields.name: Checksum
fields.desc: One's complement checksum of the structure; all zero means none was sent.

fields.name: Length
fields.desc: Object length in octets, including header and payload.
